title: I know almost nothing about coding, but I’ve been building apps with AI. What projects should I tackle next?
author: StunningProposal3579
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m a business administration student and honestly, I have almost no traditional programming background.

Over the last year, I’ve become obsessed with AI tools and started building things anyway. I’ve been using tools like Supabase, Vercel, Claude, ChatGPT, and other no-code/AI-assisted workflows to create apps and internal systems.

Some of the things I’ve worked on include:

\* Inventory management systems  
\* Personal productivity apps  
\* AI-powered dashboards  
\* Knowledge management / second-brain concepts  
\* Sports performance tracking systems  
\* Various experiments with AI agents and automation

The funny part is that I still feel like I know nothing.

I can build things that work, but I often don’t know the “proper” engineering way of doing things. Every project teaches me something new, but I feel like my knowledge is fragmented and full of gaps.

So I’m curious:

\* What projects would you recommend someone like me build next?  
\* What projects taught you the most as a developer?  
\* If you were starting today with AI tools available, what would you focus on learning?  
\* How do you organize and retain technical knowledge instead of constantly relearning things?  
\* What are the biggest blind spots people like me usually have?

I’m not necessarily trying to get a job as a developer. My goal is to become better at building useful software and eventually launch products that real people use.

I’d love to hear your suggestions, project ideas, learning paths, or even hard truths I should know.

Thanks.

comments.author: SquirrelTomahawk
comments.body:
Ima just say this.

Building apps is done in one evening.

Building a game? Oooooooh boy

replies.author: StunningProposal3579
replies.body:
That’s exactly what I’ve been realizing.

A few months ago I thought building an app was the hard part.

Now I’m learning that building the app is easy. Building a good product people actually use is the hard part.

Games still scare me though 😂

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: I'm building it in parts, self contained projects that build on each other.  And I am predicting 5 years.  I'm going to have to learn how to build a studio.  I have a plan though.

replies.author: StunningProposal3579
replies.body:
That’s actually very similar to how I’m approaching my projects.

Instead of trying to build one massive thing from day one, I’m building smaller systems that can stand on their own while also contributing to a larger vision.

The 5-year mindset is something I probably need more of. I tend to get excited about what’s possible in the next 5 weeks instead of the next 5 years.

replies.author: pennystudio
replies.body: Beat me to it, I was about to say the same thing. I built a ereader and self publishing app in one weekend. I am two months deep in the game I'm building now, no end in sight 😂

replies.author: StunningProposal3579
replies.body:
That’s exactly what I’m hearing from everyone 😂

A few months ago I thought building apps was incredibly difficult. Now it seems like the real challenge is finding users and solving meaningful problems.

Games, on the other hand, sound like a never-ending rabbit hole.

Good luck with your game. I’d love to hear what you’re building.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
For the proper engineering way of doing something, ask AI, lol.  I think AI is impowering us to all become, in business terms, founders.  I think thats right.  I would call it designers/directors.  You're job is not to create, but to guide the creation.  I have a lot of success when using AI to build my game when I can be very clear of my vision and communicate it effectively.  

As for what you should build, find a need.  What role do you want in business?  If administration is your thing, build things that make that easier/better.  Luckily, there is a lot of business software out there and I suspect AI trained with at least some of it, so it should already have the pattern of it in it's training.  But if you want to innovate, you need to come up with the idea and make it as clear as possible.  Luckily, AI can help here too.

In fact, post this to your favorite AI.  I like Claude opus.

replies.author: StunningProposal3579
replies.body:
Honestly, probably yes 😂

I've noticed some communities are still very skeptical about AI-assisted development, while others are more interested in what you're actually building.

For me, AI has been an incredible learning tool. I probably wouldn't have started building apps at all if these tools didn't exist.

And I agree with your point about being a designer/director. The more projects I work on, the more I realize that having a clear vision and understanding the problem might be more important than writing every line of code yourself.

Also, the AI-generated 3D assets idea sounds awesome. I'll definitely check that out.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body:
Stop building and start talking to customers. Make small steps and learn to sell. Learn to understand how to find problems that are big to customers. Sure building is fun but it’s irrelevant unless it solves a real problem. To be honest it’s a trap which feels a bit like a slot machine and it’s very addictive.

Instead find a problem which is super important to them. Listen to the YC combinator about hair on fire. That customer is the one you must have the skill to find.

For learning ask AI to explained everything you don’t understand on the same level and the level beneath and above, compared to what you are doing.

But important you must ground it in what you know knowledge is like a gray clay blob. If you add stuff not connected it will sin just fall to the ground and be forgotten…

replies.author: StunningProposal3579
replies.body:
I think you're right. I genuinely enjoy building things, and sometimes I probably jump into creating solutions before spending enough time validating the problem.

The "hair on fire" concept makes a lot of sense. I'm starting to realize that finding the right problem might be more important than building the solution itself.

One thing I've been trying to do recently is talk to potential users before going too deep into development, but I definitely need to get better at it.

I also really like your point about knowledge needing to connect to something real. Most of what I've learned so far has come from building projects that forced me to learn specific concepts, not from studying them in isolation.

Thanks for taking the time to write this.

comments.author: Southern_Charge5794
comments.body: Building a game for me is the most challenging vibe coding task as you literally should cover a lot of aspects and most of decisions are creative. In web and app development everything is more stable and AI can do pixel perfect design even by screenshot. Because of that those apps are looking production ready. Even without design ready you can ask Claude to implement your idea and it will work. I am doing Godot for a few month and have a lot of fun challenges that AI can't handle - dynamics. Just look at vibe coded demos here and compare how close they to production.

replies.author: Southern_Charge5794
replies.body: Good luck with game dev. My person opinion that without deep knowledge about what AI is doing your max is small demo as tech debt curve by AI there is insane.
